name: Jamal Young

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Jamal. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. Everything you tell me stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Sure, no problem. I've never done one of these, so tell me if I ramble.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work on the reconsiderations team at the regional disability benefits centre, which is an old department store they turned into offices. When someone's claim gets refused and they ask us to look again, it lands with me. I read their medical evidence, sometimes forty pages of it, ring them, ring their doctor's surgery, and write up a new decision. Kofi, who sits next to me, and I race each other to clear the oldest case on the list every Monday. The best part is overturning a bad refusal, and the worst part is the reading, because some days my eyes just stop working by three.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Okay, that's an easy one. It sounds a lot like right now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say something like, told you so, it's a fancy spell-checker. We already have a summary tool for medical reports and it's handy, but it doesn't make decisions. At five-a-side on Sunday I'd probably just say the robots aren't coming for us after all.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be fine. The job's steady, Priya's a nurse so her job's steady, and our rent is high but we cover it. The only thing that bugs me is that our pay rise has been under prices for three years running, and AI doesn't change that either way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing dramatic. I'd keep doing my cases, keep using the summary tool on the long reports, and keep putting about a hundred and fifty a month away. Maybe I'd go along to the union pay ballot this time instead of just ticking the box.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty relaxed. A bit flat, maybe, because nothing gets better either.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you use the summary tool. What do you actually use it for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly the long specialist letters. The pain clinic sends twenty-page letters. The summary tool gives me the main points in a minute, then I read the bits that matter myself. I'd never let it write the decision, but it saves my eyes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned pay falling behind prices. Does that worry you more than AI does?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Right now, yes, a bit. Priya and I want a bigger place one day, and on two public sector wages that keep falling behind, it keeps sliding away. But it's a slow worry, not a scary one.

say: I'd say AI turned out to be a **fancy spell-checker**, handy but not deciding anything.
At **five-a-side** I'd joke that the robots aren't coming for caseworkers after all.
think: My job and my partner's **nursing job** both feel steady in this picture.
The real niggle is **pay rises** falling behind prices for three years.
do: Keep using the **summary tool** on long medical reports but write decisions myself.
Keep saving about **a hundred and fifty** a month.
Vote in the **union pay ballot** instead of just ticking the box.
feel: **Relaxed**, with a slightly flat feeling that nothing gets better either.
S0.quote: The pain clinic sends twenty-page letters. The summary tool gives me the main points in a minute, then I read the bits that matter myself.
fieldNote: He already uses AI **lightly and carefully**, as a reading aid rather than a decision-maker.
His real background worry is **pay falling behind** prices, not technology.
Two **steady public sector incomes** make this picture feel genuinely secure.

steps.text: Keep using the summary tool only on long specialist letters
Put about a hundred and fifty a month into savings
Vote in the union pay ballot this year

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Right. That's the one where the summary tool starts writing the decisions too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say we need the union in the room before the rollout, not after. Online I'd probably share stuff about disabled people getting wrongly refused by automated systems in other countries. I'd keep it measured, though, because I'm not the shouting type.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, my job is mostly reading and writing, so I think the team gets cut. Not all of us, but if one person with good software can do what three of us do now, they'll keep the one. I'm average at this job, not the best, and when they're choosing who to keep, the middle is the worst place to be.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First I'd get properly good at the new tools, because once Kofi and the others are using them I'd want to be the one who can check them fast. I'd up my savings to two hundred a month and skip the trip to see my cousins abroad. And I'd ask the welfare rights centre in town about volunteering on Saturdays, to see if advice work suits me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit sick in the stomach. I'm not panicking, but I'd be checking the team list every month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you're average at the job. Who would they keep?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably people like Joanne, who knows the regulations inside out, and the young ones who are quick with the software. I'm in the middle on both.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Priya that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell her it's not the end of the world but we should hold off on looking at bigger flats for a year. She'd say her hospital is crying out for people and I could retrain. I'd say I faint at blood tests, and we'd laugh, but she'd have a point.

say: I'd say the **union** needs to be in the room before any rollout, not after.
Online I'd share stories of **disabled people** wrongly refused by automated systems elsewhere.
think: My job is mostly **reading and writing**, so I expect the team to be cut.
Being **average** at the job puts me in the worst place when they choose who stays.
do: Get good at the **new tools** so I can check their decisions quickly.
Raise saving to **two hundred a month** and skip the trip to see my cousins.
Volunteer on **Saturdays** at the welfare rights centre to test advice work.
feel: A **sick feeling** in the stomach, short of panic.
**Watchful**, checking the team list every month.
S1.quote: I'm average at this job, not the best, and when they're choosing who to keep, the middle is the worst place to be.
fieldNote: He frames the threat as **who gets kept**, and sees himself honestly as middling.
His steady streak shows: he'd learn the tools once **colleagues** are using them.
His partner's **nursing job** comes up as a fallback he jokes about but doesn't dismiss.

steps.text: Learn the new decision tools well enough to check them fast
Raise saving to two hundred a month and skip the cousins trip
Volunteer Saturdays at the town's welfare rights centre
Hold off on looking at bigger flats for a year

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. Wow. That's basically my next two pay reviews.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Publicly I'd back whatever the unions call for, a pause, a guaranteed income, all of it. I'd go to the march. I'd say on every group chat that a machine deciding if someone is disabled enough is a line we shouldn't cross without a vote.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'm out of a job by 2029. Everything I do is thinking work, and the hands-on robots coming three years later only matters for people like Priya. My skills, reading files and writing decisions, are exactly what this kind of AI is for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop all spending that isn't rent and food, today. I'd ask HR about the redundancy terms in writing, and then I'd look hard at the hospital's healthcare assistant scheme, where they train you on the job, because that's hands-on and buys me a few years. I'd also lean on the union, because two years is too fast for anyone to make a plan alone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared. Properly scared, the kind where you don't sleep and you scroll job sites at two in the morning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You joked earlier about fainting at blood tests. Is the hospital scheme real for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It'd have to be. I'd rather learn to cope with blood than sit at home. Priya would help me get through it, and the pay is lower but it's a pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How long would your savings last?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe four months of my half of the rent and bills. Priya's wage would carry us for a while after that, but not forever, and I'd hate being the one who isn't paying in.

say: I'd back union calls for a **pause** and a guaranteed income, and join the march.
I'd say a machine deciding **who is disabled enough** shouldn't happen without a vote.
think: I expect to be **out of a job** by 2029, since all my work is thinking work.
The **robot delay** protects my partner's hospital job, not my desk.
do: Cut all spending except **rent and food**, starting today.
Ask HR for **redundancy terms** in writing.
Apply to the hospital's **healthcare assistant** training scheme.
feel: **Properly scared**, scrolling job sites at two in the morning.
S2.quote: My skills, reading files and writing decisions, are exactly what this kind of AI is for.
fieldNote: He sees the **thinking-first order** as decisive: his job goes, his partner's buys time.
He'd move into **hands-on care** despite disliking blood, which shows how serious he finds it.
Savings cover about **four months** of his share before his partner carries them.

steps.text: Cut spending to rent and food only
Ask HR for redundancy terms in writing
Apply to the hospital's on-the-job healthcare assistant scheme
Back the union's call for a pause and guaranteed income

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. That's more room, but I'd still only be thirty-two when it lands.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the same things as with the fast one, but more calmly: five years is enough time to plan, so there's no excuse for the government not to. I'd want a retraining fund announced in the first year, not the fourth.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, five years means I can wait a bit. I move once I see how it's going for others, never first and never last. My worry is that by the time it's proven, the good spots are taken.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start an evening course in something people-facing, probably the welfare rights advice certificate, and keep using the tools at work so I understand them. I'd save three hundred a month for two years so I've got a cushion when I jump. Around 2029 I'd make the move, either into advice work or the hospital.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, mostly. There's a timer running, but I can see it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Advice work is still thinking work. Isn't that exposed too?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yeah, you're right, I hadn't really put that together. The part that isn't exposed is sitting with someone who's crying in a tribunal waiting room. Maybe I need a job that's more of that and less of the paperwork.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you watch to know when to move?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Kofi, honestly. He always tries things first. If he's moved and he's doing alright by 2029, that's my sign.

say: I'd say five years means the government has **no excuse** not to plan.
I'd want a **retraining fund** announced in the first year, not the fourth.
think: I move once I see **how others fare**, never first and never last.
My worry is that by the time it's proven, the **good spots** are taken.
do: Start an **evening course** in welfare rights advice.
Save **three hundred a month** for two years before making a move.
Plan the jump into **advice or hospital work** around 2029.
feel: **Uneasy** and watching a timer he can at least see.
S3.quote: I move once I see how it's going for others, never first and never last. My worry is that by the time it's proven, the good spots are taken.
fieldNote: His **steady** style shows clearly: he'd watch his colleague Kofi and move second.
A follow-up exposed that **advice work** is also thinking work, which he hadn't considered.
He lands on wanting **people-facing** work over paperwork as the safer part.

steps.text: Take the evening welfare rights advice certificate
Save three hundred a month for two years
Keep using the casework AI tools to understand their limits
Move into advice work or hospital care around 2029

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years is a long time. I'd be thirty-seven, maybe with kids by then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell people at work this is the one where nobody has an excuse to be surprised. I'd say it on the union page too: ten years is enough for every benefits office to have a plan for every person in it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be okay for the first few years and then I'd need to have moved. The good thing about ten years is I could retrain properly instead of grabbing whatever's going. The bad thing is I might put it off. That's what I do with things that aren't urgent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd talk to Priya seriously about nursing, because her hospital funds the training and she'd help me through it. I'd start the access course around 2028 and qualify by about 2032, which still leaves years before robots reach hands-on care. Meanwhile I'd keep my caseworker job and keep saving.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Okay, with a nagging feeling. Like a dentist appointment far away that you know you'll still dread.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you might put it off. What would make you actually start?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A date in the diary and someone checking on me, which would be Priya. If I sign up for the access course in 2027, I'll do it. If I just say I'll do it someday, I won't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would ten years change plans like kids or buying a home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd probably still have kids, but maybe a couple of years later, once I've switched. I don't want to be retraining with a baby and a mortgage at the same time.

say: I'd say this is the picture where **nobody** has an excuse to be surprised.
I'd post that every benefits office needs a **plan for every person** in it.
think: Ten years lets me **retrain properly** instead of grabbing whatever is going.
My risk is **putting it off**, because I do that with things that aren't urgent.
do: Start a **nursing access course** around 2028 and qualify by about 2032.
Keep my **caseworker job** and keep saving while training.
Delay **having children** until after the switch.
feel: **Okay**, with a **nagging feeling**, like a distant appointment he'll still dread.
S4.quote: The good thing about ten years is I could retrain properly instead of grabbing whatever's going. The bad thing is I might put it off.
fieldNote: He's honest that **procrastination** is his biggest risk with a long runway.
His partner's **hospital** becomes the concrete route, with funded training and support.
The timeline pushes back **children** by a couple of years.

steps.text: Sign up for a nursing access course in 2027
Keep the caseworker job and saving while training
Delay having children until after qualifying as a nurse

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because two years isn't enough to retrain into anything real, and I'd be grabbing whatever came. What would help is the government paying people like me to train while still on salary, the way the hospital pays nurses to train. That one thing would change everything.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe how it feels to be the person who decides on someone's disability claim. A refusal letter decides whether someone can pay the heating. I'd want whatever replaces me to know that, and I'm not sure it can.

headlineQuote: A refusal letter decides whether someone can pay the heating. I'd want whatever replaces me to know that, and I'm not sure it can.
portrait: Jamal is a 27-year-old caseworker who **reconsiders refused disability claims** at a regional benefits centre.
He uses a **summary tool** on long medical letters but writes every decision himself.
He sees himself as **average** at the job, which makes him fear cuts in the steady picture.
In the AGI pictures he'd move toward **hands-on care**, helped by his nurse partner.
He's **steady**, waiting to see colleagues move first, and admits he puts off non-urgent things.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because two years is too short to retrain into anything real.
whatWouldHelp: **Paid training on salary**, like the hospital offers nurses.
